claims.text: Nitrogen doping will mitigate activity loss and structural degradation under transient, low-temperature automotive exhaust conditions.
The nitrogen-doped catalyst will maintain low platinum consumption.
The starting catalyst is a nearly equiatomic, homogeneous solid-solution alloy containing multiple principal elements and platinum-group metals.
Thermal annealing in a nitrogen-containing atmosphere or NH3 followed by mild acid etching will incorporate nitrogen into the catalyst.
The proposed treatment will generate stable metal–nitrogen bonds.
The proposed treatment will cause platinum to segregate to the surface and form a self-assembled Pt-rich shell.
Chemically stable M–N bonds suppress transition-metal dissolution and oxidation.
A Pt-rich outer shell inhibits platinum dissolution.
M–N bonding and the Pt-rich shell hinder particle coarsening.
Doped nitrogen induces local lattice distortion.
Nitrogen-induced lattice distortion suppresses metal-atom diffusion and thereby improves durability.
Nitrogen incorporation redistributes charge and optimizes the electronic structure of surface platinum.
Nitrogen-induced electronic modification of surface platinum inhibits dissolution of the Pt shell.
The proposed protective structure will resist dissolution during exposure to H2O, NO, and thermal cycling.
The treated catalyst will retain activity better and exhibit improved long-term durability relative to the untreated catalyst.
The treated catalyst will have a lower platinum dissolution rate than the untreated catalyst.
The untreated automotive catalyst loses activity through nanoparticle coarsening, metal dissolution, and phase changes under the stated exhaust conditions.
Excessive nitrogen doping or over-annealing can cause undesirable phase transformations or excessive segregation that impair catalytic activity.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as a single treatment step, but it consists of two sequential operations: nitrogen-atmosphere annealing followed by acid etching.
